TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation
from Model Behaviors

Jiayi Chen Email: jiayichen25@m.fudan.edu.cn    Hui Li Email: maxmpan@tencent.com    Yujiong Shen Email: tgui@fudan.edu.cn    Qiyuan Peng    Yanxin Li    Chenhao Huang    Shaofan Liu    Guoqiang Zhang    Junjie Ye    Shihan Dou    Ming Zhang    Maxm Pan    Tao Gui    Qi Zhang    Xuanjing Huang    Fudan University Hunyuan Team    Tencent
Abstract

Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model’s underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100%100\% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%83.3\%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8%77.8\% versus 88.9%88.9\%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.

1 Introduction

Public benchmarks now anchor nearly every comparison between large language models (LLMs), with leaderboard rankings directly shaping deployment choices and research priorities (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026b). Comparisons on these benchmarks are routinely reduced to a single aggregate score that carries limited information about a model’s underlying capabilities (Murahari et al., 2024; Dehghani et al., 2021; Dou et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026d). A low score signals overall weakness but not which specific directions to improve on, while a high score does not reveal which capabilities a model has actually mastered. Two models with nearly identical aggregate scores can follow qualitatively different capability profiles, and no scalar reveals why one model outperforms another or where its weaknesses lie. What is needed is a general paradigm that treats the evaluation result itself, rather than its aggregate scalar, as the supervision signal for fine-grained capability structure (Burnell et al., 2023; Mizrahi et al., 2024). Figure 1 illustrates this gap, with frontier models collapsing into a narrow band at the aggregate level yet sharply separated on the fine-grained capability slices that TIDE exposes.

Existing fine-grained methods rely on external sources, benchmark metadata or flat LLM weakness lists, which fix granularity in advance and rarely align with each model’s capability boundary (Hendrycks et al., 2020; Murahari et al., 2024). Recent hierarchical methods induce capability trees (Zeng et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025) but from external taxonomies or semantic similarity, leaving model behavior unused as the supervision signal for the tree itself.

Taking a behavioral perspective, we frame fine-grained capability diagnosis as supervised structure discovery over model behavior. This naturally instantiates as decision-tree induction (Breiman et al., 2017; Quinlan, 1986), since benchmark samples are heterogeneous and model behavior differs at nested levels of granularity. We therefore propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), a decision-tree induction method. At each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate split rules from the sample content, and a behavior-based information gain selects among them. The LLM serves only as the hypothesis generator, while the behavior matrix supplies the supervision (full procedure in Section 4). The resulting capability tree has behavior-aligned, fine-grained capability slices at every node. This behavior supervision distinguishes TIDE from unsupervised sample clustering (McQueen, 1967; Ward Jr, 1963; Zhang et al., 2023), which groups samples on semantic similarity alone.

We apply TIDE to profile five frontier models across four benchmarks, where it produces dev-to-test consistent weakness rankings with worst-leaf accuracy drops up to 37.9137.91, amplifies small aggregate gaps into substantially larger leaf-level contrasts, and yields diagnostic trees that transfer across benchmarks. Our ablation analysis further isolates the behavior-based information gain, rather than the LLM rule pool alone, as the key diagnostic signal. Used as a fine-grained probe, TIDE uncovers capability findings invisible at the aggregate level, such as a 16.716.7 leaf-level gap on microeconomic market reasoning between Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 on MMLU-Pro, and a 41.241.2 regression on large-number computation from GPT-5.2 to GPT-5.4 on DROP. Our contributions can be summarized as follows

  • •

    We reframe fine-grained diagnostic evaluation as supervised structure discovery over model behavior and define a behavior-based information gain that combines intra-model consistency with inter-model separability as the supervision signal.

  • •

    We propose TIDE, a decision-tree induction method that strictly decouples an LLM hypothesis generator from behavior-based split selection, producing a hierarchical capability tree whose nodes are behavior-aligned capability slices.

  • •

    Across five models on four benchmarks, TIDE yields consistent weakness rankings, transferable diagnostic trees, and capability findings invisible at the aggregate level, with our ablation analysis isolating behavior-based selection as the key signal. These results position TIDE as a building block for behavior-supervised, fine-grained evaluation of frontier models.

2 Related Work

LLM Benchmarking.

LLM evaluation has been dominated by standardized benchmarks that span knowledge and reasoning (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2024; Phan et al., 2025; Dou et al., 2026a; Dou et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026a), instruction following (Zhou et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024), and head-to-head model comparison (Li et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023), whose leaderboards rank models by a single aggregate score and shape deployment and research decisions. However, an aggregate scalar carries little information about which capabilities a model has mastered or where its weaknesses lie, motivating the fine-grained capability diagnosis discussed next.

Fine-Grained Capability Diagnosis.

Early efforts characterize capabilities through external sources, including benchmark metadata (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2020; Suzgun et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), LLM-discovered capability attributes (Murahari et al., 2024), or automated topic grouping (Chiang et al., 2024), alongside checklists (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2025) and robustness evaluation (Morris et al., 2020; Goel et al., 2021). However, such metadata is often unavailable (Li et al., 2023; Dubois et al., 2024) and fixed at a granularity poorly aligned with each model’s capability boundary, while flat-list methods conflate category frequency with weakness. Recent hierarchical methods automate tree construction, with EvalTree (Zeng et al., 2025) clustering embeddings top-down and SkillVerse (Tian et al., 2025) deriving dendrograms from LLM critiques. Both rely on semantic similarity rather than model behavior as the supervision signal for the tree. TIDE adapts decision-tree induction (Breiman et al., 2017; Quinlan, 1986) to this setting: an LLM proposes semantic split rules while a behavior matrix selects which rule to retain, making split selection behavior-grounded.

3 Problem Formulation

Why View Diagnostic Evaluation as Behavior-Supervised Tree Induction?

Given a benchmark ℬ={xi}i=1N\mathcal{B}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and a set ℳ={mj}j=1M\mathcal{M}=\{m_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} of evaluated models, a deterministic judge assigns a scalar score Yj,i∈[0,1]Y_{j,i}\in[0,1] to each (model, sample) pair, abstracting the rubric, accuracy, or pass-rate definition adopted by the benchmark. These scores together form the behavior matrix Y∈[0,1]M×NY\in[0,1]^{M\times N}. We view fine-grained diagnostic evaluation as supervised structure discovery over model behavior: YY is the only supervision signal, while the samples themselves remain natural-language objects without pre-existing feature representations.

This view naturally instantiates as tree induction. Benchmark samples are heterogeneous along multiple semantic axes and model behavior differs at nested levels of granularity, so a hierarchy of progressively finer subsets matches both the data and the supervision better than any flat partition. We model the output as a tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} in which each node vv corresponds to a sample subset Bv⊆ℬB_{v}\subseteq\mathcal{B} with Broot=ℬB_{\mathrm{root}}=\mathcal{B}, every internal node carries a human-readable split rule rvr_{v} describing how its children partition BvB_{v}, and every leaf inherits its identity from the conjunction of split rules along its root-to-leaf path. What remains is to specify what makes a split of Bv⊆ℬB_{v}\subseteq\mathcal{B} behaviorally informative, which is quantified by a behavior-based split objective.

Behavior-Based Split Objective.

We define a behavior-based split objective that combines intra-model consistency and inter-model separability, scoring each candidate KK-way partition π\pi of Bv⊆ℬB_{v}\subseteq\mathcal{B} by how well its children improve both desiderata. We adopt the standard decision-tree information gain template (Definition 1) and instantiate it with two complementary impurities (Definitions 2 and 3).

Definition 1.

For a KK-way partition π={B1,…,BK}\pi=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{K}\} of BB with wk=|Bk|/|B|w_{k}=|B_{k}|/|B|, the information gain under impurity ϕ\phi is

Δϕ​(π)=ϕ⁡(B)−∑k=1Kwk​ϕ​(Bk).\Delta_{\phi}(\pi)=\phi(B)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\,\phi(B_{k}). (1)
Definition 2.

Intra-model gain. For a single model mjm_{j}, the within-set variance on BB is

Varj​(B)=1|B|​∑i∈B(Yj,i−Y¯j​(B))2,\mathrm{Var}_{j}(B)=\tfrac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\bigl(Y_{j,i}-\bar{Y}_{j}(B)\bigr)^{2}, (2)

where Y¯j​(B)=|B|−1​∑i∈BYj,i\bar{Y}_{j}(B)=|B|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B}Y_{j,i}. Averaging across ℳ\mathcal{M} yields the impurity

V¯​(B)=1M​∑j=1MVarj​(B),\bar{V}(B)=\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\mathrm{Var}_{j}(B), (3)

and the corresponding gain is

IntraGain⁡(π)=ΔV¯​(π).\mathrm{IntraGain}(\pi)=\Delta_{\bar{V}}(\pi). (4)

A large IntraGain\mathrm{IntraGain} indicates that, within each child subset, every model behaves more consistently than on the parent, so the split groups samples that elicit similar behavior from the same model.

Definition 3.

Inter-model gain. The dispersion of per-model means on BB is

Sep⁡(B)=1M​∑j=1M(Y¯j​(B)−Y¯​(B))2,\mathrm{Sep}(B)=\tfrac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\bigl(\bar{Y}_{j}(B)-\bar{Y}(B)\bigr)^{2}, (5)

where Y¯​(B)=M−1​∑j=1MY¯j​(B)\bar{Y}(B)=M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\bar{Y}_{j}(B) is the average across models. Since dispersion should increase after the split, the inter-model gain is its negation:

InterGain⁡(π)=−ΔSep​(π).\mathrm{InterGain}(\pi)=-\Delta_{\mathrm{Sep}}(\pi). (6)

A large InterGain\mathrm{InterGain} indicates that the per-model averages are more spread out inside each child than on the parent, exposing subsets where model contrasts are pronounced rather than washed out by aggregation.

Unified criterion.

We combine the two desiderata into the behavior-based information gain:

𝒢⁡(π)=α​IntraGain​(π)+α¯​InterGain​(π),\mathcal{G}(\pi)=\alpha\,\mathrm{IntraGain}(\pi)+\bar{\alpha}\,\mathrm{InterGain}(\pi), (7)

where α¯=1−α\bar{\alpha}=1-\alpha and α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) trades consistency for separability. When evaluating a single model (M=1M=1), Sep≡0\mathrm{Sep}\equiv 0 and 𝒢\mathcal{G} collapses to IntraGain\mathrm{IntraGain} regardless of α\alpha, recovering single-model weakness localization as a special case. A discussion of why we score splits by behavior variation rather than error frequency is deferred to Appendix B.

4 Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation

4.1 Overview

TIDE constructs the capability tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} from (ℬ,Y)(\mathcal{B},Y) by top-down recursive splitting. Figure 2 illustrates the overall pipeline. Starting from Broot=ℬB_{\mathrm{root}}=\mathcal{B}, at each node with subset BB we (i) prompt an LLM judge to generate CC candidate split rules from the sample content of BB (Section 4.2), (ii) score every candidate by the behavior-based split objective 𝒢\mathcal{G} (Section 3) combined with a balance regularizer (Section 4.3), (iii) keep the highest-scoring feasible candidate, and (iv) recurse on its children until stopping criteria are met (Section 4.4). The full pseudocode is deferred to Appendix A.

4.2 LLM-Generated Candidate Partitions

At each node, the LLM produces CC candidate partitions in two stages: a split-rule proposer generates CC candidate split rules from the local sample subset, and a classifier routes samples into groups under each rule, yielding CC candidate partitions {πc}c=1C\{\pi_{c}\}_{c=1}^{C} that Section 4.3 then compares.

Split-rule generation.

The split-rule proposer takes a sample subset B⊆ℬB\subseteq\mathcal{B} and proposes CC candidate split rules 𝒞={c1,…,cC}\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{C}\}. Each split rule cc consists of a natural-language criterion specifying a sample-side axis and LcL_{c} mutually exclusive groups indexed by j∈{1,…,Lc}j\in\{1,\dots,L_{c}\} with 2≤Lc≤52\leq L_{c}\leq 5, each carrying a generalizable description. The proposer is prompted to consider complementary axes including ability type, domain and topic, cognitive level (Bloom, 1956; Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001), solution strategy, complexity, knowledge source, answer format, and constraint structure. Crucially, the proposer sees only the sample text and reference answer of each x∈Bx\in B and never any model output, so each split rule characterizes the capability demanded by the samples in BB rather than summarizing evaluation outcomes on them.

Sample classification.

For each candidate cc, the classifier assigns every x∈Bx\in B to exactly one group j∈{1,…,Lc}j\in\{1,\dots,L_{c}\}, inducing disjoint subsets Bc,j⊆BB_{c,j}\subseteq B that together form a partition πc={Bc,1,…,Bc,Lc}\pi_{c}=\{B_{c,1},\dots,B_{c,L_{c}}\}. The behavior matrix YY is consulted only once we score {πc}c=1C\{\pi_{c}\}_{c=1}^{C} in Section 4.3.

4.3 Behavior-Based Split Selection

Among the CC candidates, we choose the split that maximizes the behavior-based information gain 𝒢⁡(πc)\mathcal{G}(\pi_{c}) from Equation 7. However, the gain aggregates child-level impurities with weights proportional to subset size, so optimizing 𝒢\mathcal{G} alone systematically rewards splits in which one or two groups absorb most samples while the remaining groups are left with only a handful of items, which are too sparse to be representative of a meaningful capability slice. To rule out such splits, we complement 𝒢\mathcal{G} with a balance regularizer (Breiman et al., 2017; Von Luxburg, 2007). Let n¯c=|B|/Lc\bar{n}_{c}=|B|/L_{c} denote the expected group size under a uniform split and define

Balancec=minj=1Lc​|Bc,j|n¯c∈[0,1].\mathrm{Balance}_{c}\;=\;\min_{j=1}^{L_{c}}\frac{|B_{c,j}|}{\bar{n}_{c}}\,\in[0,1]. (8)

The effective score of candidate cc is

𝒮c=𝒢⁡(πc)⋅Balancecβ.\mathcal{S}_{c}\;=\;\mathcal{G}(\pi_{c})\cdot\mathrm{Balance}_{c}^{\,\beta}. (9)

We further require every group to contain at least nminn_{\min} samples and let 𝒞valid={c∈𝒞:minj⁡|Bc,j|≥nmin}\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{valid}}=\{c\in\mathcal{C}:\min_{j}|B_{c,j}|\geq n_{\min}\} denote the feasible candidates. The selected split is

c⋆=arg⁡maxc∈𝒞valid⁡𝒮c.c^{\star}\;=\;\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{valid}}}\,\mathcal{S}_{c}. (10)

4.4 Recursive Tree Construction and Stopping Criteria

Starting from B=ℬB=\mathcal{B} at depth zero, we apply Sections 4.2 and 4.3 to the current node’s subset and recurse on each child Bc⋆,jB_{c^{\star},j} at depth d+1d+1. Recursion at a node terminates as soon as any of the following holds: (i) the maximum depth dmaxd_{\max} is reached; (ii) the node subset is too small, |B|<nmin|B|<n_{\min}; or (iii) every feasible split yields insufficient gain, that is, 𝒞valid=∅\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{valid}}=\emptyset or maxc∈𝒞valid⁡𝒮c<gmin\max_{c\in\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{valid}}}\mathcal{S}_{c}<g_{\min} for a minimum effective-gain threshold gming_{\min}.

4.5 Diagnostic Extraction from the Induced Tree

A constructed tree 𝒯\mathcal{T} is directly usable for diagnosis: traversing it top-down, we keep nodes whose behavior statistic deviates substantially from the root, with a single evaluated model the statistic is the within-node mean s⁡(Bv)=Y¯m​(Bv)s(B_{v})=\bar{Y}_{m}(B_{v}) and qualifying nodes (those significantly below s⁡(Broot)s(B_{\mathrm{root}})) localize weaknesses, while with multiple models the statistic is the cross-model gap g⁡(Bv)=maxm⁡Y¯m​(Bv)−minm⁡Y¯m​(Bv)g(B_{v})=\max_{m}\bar{Y}_{m}(B_{v})-\min_{m}\bar{Y}_{m}(B_{v}) and qualifying nodes (those significantly above g⁡(Broot)g(B_{\mathrm{root}})) localize discriminative slices. Along each branch we descend into qualifying children when they exist and otherwise record the current node, so the report contains the most specific weak or discriminative node per branch. The precise statistical test is given in Appendix C.2.1.

5 Experiment

We organize the analysis around six research questions: RQ1-3 test the core diagnostic capabilities of TIDE on held-out stability, pairwise discrimination, and cross-benchmark transfer; RQ4-5 use it as a microscope for model insights across near-tied models and within-family versions; and RQ6 ablates the behavior-based selection signal.

Datasets and Models. We evaluate TIDE on MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), and BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022); MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020) is used for cross-benchmark transfer. For each benchmark, we sample 3,000 items and evenly split them into dev and test sets. Trees are constructed using only the dev set. We test Grok 4.20 (xAI, 2025), Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2025), DeepSeek-V3.2 (Liu et al., 2025), GPT-5.4 (Singh et al., 2025), Qwen-Plus (Bai et al., 2023), and GPT-5.2. See Appendix D.

Baselines. We compare against two LLM-flat methods, TextDiff (Zhong et al., 2022) and QualEval (Murahari et al., 2024), and two hierarchical methods, EvalTree (Zeng et al., 2025) and SkillVerse (Tian et al., 2025), covering the two main paradigms of prior fine-grained diagnostic work.

Metrics. We evaluate diagnostic trees along four axes, with symbols matching Section 4.5.

  • •

    Weakness consistency (ρ\rho): the Spearman rank (Spearman, 1961) correlation between dev-set and test-set severity rankings over weak nodes, measuring stability on held-out items.

  • •

    Weak-leaf drop (Δ=Accagg−Accweak\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{agg}}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{weak}}): the gap between the model’s aggregate accuracy and its accuracy on the extracted weak leaves (selection procedure in Appendix D), measuring the severity of the localized failures.

  • •

    Model-discrimination gaps: for a pair of models, Δglobal\Delta_{\text{global}} is the absolute aggregate-accuracy gap and Δleaf\Delta_{\text{leaf}} is the largest leaf-level gap.

  • •

    Cross-benchmark transfer accuracy: route target items through a source-benchmark tree and report Δ=Accagg−Accweak\Delta=\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{agg}}-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{weak}} on the target side, measuring whether source-induced weak leaves isolate target failures.

5.1 Main Results

RQ1: Can TIDE reliably identify model weaknesses?

Table 1 reports two metrics: weakness consistency ρ\rho, which measures whether weak leaves on dev remain weak on held-out items, and weak-leaf drop Δ\Delta, which measures how much lower the weak leaf’s accuracy is compared to the aggregate score.

Finding 1: TIDE delivers weak-leaf diagnostics whose relative ordering is preserved on held-out items. The two baselines in Table 1 typically satisfy only one of these requirements. TextDiff often shows high ρ\rho paired with a small Δ\Delta, e.g., on BBH, suggesting reproducible partitions that nevertheless do not isolate a real localized weakness; EvalTree shows the mirror pattern on MMLU-Pro, with a sizeable Δ\Delta but near-zero ρ\rho, suggesting that its weak leaves are fitted to the construction split and do not transfer to test. TIDE sits closer to the ideal regime: it ranks among the top two on ρ\rho in the majority of settings, reaching 0.940.94–1.001.00 on BBH and DROP, while at the same time producing the largest weak-leaf drop. Taken together, these two metrics indicate that the weak leaves identified by TIDE correspond to a genuine capability gap of the underlying model rather than an artifact of a single split.

RQ2: For pairwise model comparison, can TIDE reveal where two models actually differ?

Beyond single-model diagnosis, TIDE can also be used to compare two models. Figure 4 compares Qwen-Plus and DeepSeek-V3.2, whose aggregate scores are close on most benchmarks.

Finding 2: TIDE amplifies small aggregate gaps into large, interpretable leaf-level contrasts. As shown in Figure 4, the leaf-level gap Δleaf\Delta_{\text{leaf}} is consistently much larger than the aggregate gap Δglobal\Delta_{\text{global}} across all four benchmarks. The relative gap gain ranges from +117%+117\% on MMLU-Pro to +684%+684\% on BBQ, where the aggregate gap is only 3.33.3 but the leaf-level gap reaches 25.625.6. This shows that TIDE can move model comparison beyond a single aggregate ranking to pinpointing which specific capability regions separate two models.

RQ3: Can the diagnostic tree transfer across benchmarks?

Beyond diagnosing within a single benchmark, we further test whether the tree structure is transferable. We induce tree on the dev split of one benchmark, route test items from another benchmark through it, and report the weakest-leaf accuracy on the target benchmark in Table 2.

Finding 3: The diagnostic tree generalizes across benchmarks. In both transfer directions between MMLU and MMLU-Pro, every model exhibits a positive worst-leaf drop Δ\Delta, ranging from 1.611.61 to 11.7411.74. This means that weak leaves discovered on one benchmark continue to isolate genuinely harder slices on a different benchmark, even though the tree never observed any target-side examples. The result suggests splits found by TIDE capture underlying capability boundaries rather than benchmark-specific surface patterns, making the diagnostic tree reusable across evaluation settings.

5.2 Model Insights via TIDE

RQ4: When two models score nearly the same, where does TIDE reveal they actually differ?

We take GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.6 on MMLU-Pro as a concrete case study. Their aggregate accuracies are 85.2%85.2\% versus 86.2%86.2\%, with an aggregate gap of only 1.01.0. MMLU-Pro is suitable for this analysis because it covers diverse disciplinary skills, so similar aggregate scores can arise from very different capability profiles.

Finding 4: TIDE decomposes a near-tie into clear per-capability contrasts. As shown in the left panel of Figure 3, Claude Opus 4.6 is stronger on microeconomic market reasoning, civil liability reasoning, multi-step computation, mechanics reasoning, and anatomical structure reasoning, while GPT-5.4 is stronger on contract law reasoning. The largest leaf-level gap reaches 19.119.1 on anatomical structure reasoning, where GPT-5.4 achieves 61.9%61.9\% and Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 81.0%81.0\%. These per-leaf contrasts provide actionable information that a single aggregate score or pairwise win rate cannot offer, directly indicating which capabilities should be prioritized in deployment or further evaluation.

RQ5: Can TIDE track capability changes within the same model family?

We compare GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.4 on DROP to test whether TIDE can reveal capability-level changes within the same model family. Their aggregate accuracies differ by only 0.70.7, but the per-leaf comparison exposes much larger shifts.

Finding 5: Model updates can improve some capabilities while degrading others. As shown in the right panel of Figure 3, GPT-5.4 improves over GPT-5.2 on person extraction and location extraction, but drops on single-team sports aggregation, touchdown counting, large-number computation, and basic arithmetic. The largest gap reaches 41.241.2 on large-number computation, despite the aggregate gap being only 0.70.7. This suggests that version comparisons within a model family are better audited at the capability level: a newer release may match the older version in aggregate accuracy while silently losing accuracy on a handful of specific capability leaves, which a single aggregate score would conceal.

5.3 Ablation Analysis

RQ6: Does behavior-based information gain add signal beyond the LLM rule-proposal pool?

We ablate the rule-selection mechanism while keeping the same LLM-generated candidate pool, so that performance differences can be attributed to how the tree chooses among proposed partitions rather than to better rule generation. Table 3 reports weakness consistency ρ\rho and worst-leaf drop Δ\Delta for each variant.

Finding 6: Rule proposal alone is insufficient; behavior-based selection is the key diagnostic signal. As shown in Table 3, TIDE achieves the strongest results, with ρ=0.94\rho=0.94 and Δ=13.59\Delta=13.59. Random selection retains a similar ρ\rho but reduces Δ\Delta from 13.5913.59 to 1.531.53, confirming the importance of behavior-based selection. Removing the balance regularizer drops ρ\rho to 0.550.55, suggesting that highly imbalanced leaves yield unstable estimates across dev and test. The α\alpha sweep and the gain-component ablation analysis further show that both intra-model consistency and inter-model separability are necessary. Together, these results support the balanced default as the most reliable setting.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we first reframe fine-grained diagnostic evaluation as supervised structure discovery over model behavior. We then propose TIDE, a decision-tree induction method in which an LLM judge proposes candidate split rules and a behavior-based information gain selects among them. Experimental results on five frontier models across four benchmarks show that TIDE produces consistent weakness rankings, transferable diagnostic trees, and capability findings invisible at the aggregate level. Our ablation analysis further confirms that behavior-based selection is the key diagnostic signal. We hope TIDE extends aggregate scoring with finer-grained diagnostic information, and that behavior-supervised capability trees become a building block for diagnosing frontier models.

Limitations

Although TIDE provides a fine-grained diagnostic view, it still has several limitations. First, TIDE relies on repeated LLM calls for split-rule generation and sample classification at every node, which incurs non-trivial API cost. We mitigate this by parallelizing classification across multiple workers and caching outputs at every stage, and the induced tree can be reused across additional evaluated models without re-induction. Second, our experiments focus on static, single-turn English benchmarks evaluated by a deterministic scorer, and we have not validated TIDE on multi-turn dialogues, agentic settings, or open-ended generation. The framework itself is benchmark-agnostic, and extending the behavior matrix to richer signals such as per-turn rewards or rubric-based scores is a natural direction for future work. Third, the quality of the induced tree depends on the LLM serving as both split proposer and classifier. We believe, however, that current frontier LLMs are sufficiently strong, owing to their extensive prior knowledge, to support reliable split-rule generation and sample classification, and our ablation analysis further isolates behavior-based selection rather than the LLM split pool as the key diagnostic signal, suggesting robustness to moderate variation in backbone choice.

Appendix A Algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes the recursive construction procedure of TIDE described in Section 4.

Appendix B Why Behavior, Not Error Frequency

The behavior-based information gain scores a candidate split rule by how model behavior varies within and across models on its children, not by how many errors the subset accumulates. When every model fails on the same samples, the subset has many errors yet small within-model variance and small between-model contrast, so the gain stays near zero and the tree does not descend along such branches. Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation thereby distinguishes subsets that reveal model-specific weakness from those that are merely uniformly hard, avoiding the conflation of error frequency with weakness that arises when diagnosis inspects only failed instances.

Appendix C Implementation Details

C.1 Baseline Implementations

We compare against four representative weakness profiling methods spanning different paradigms of automated LLM capability diagnosis. All baselines use GPT-5.2 as the backbone LLM unless otherwise noted. Following the shared dev-test protocol, each dataset is split evenly: the first half serves as the development (training) set for weakness identification, and the second half serves as the held-out test set for evaluation.

EvalTree (Zeng et al., 2025).

EvalTree constructs a hierarchical capability tree over benchmark instances. Each internal node represents a natural-language capability description and is associated with a subset of instances that specifically test that capability, leaf nodes correspond to individual instances. The tree is built top-down via recursive clustering of instance embeddings, with capability labels generated by an LLM at each node (Figure 6). Weakness profiling proceeds by identifying nodes whose associated instances yield significantly low model accuracy under EvalTree’s default threshold on the development set, then collecting these node descriptions as the weakness profile. We use EvalTree’s official implementation with default hyperparameters and stopping criteria. The profile ordering follows the node extraction sequence output by the method, which we treat as the predicted weakness ranking. Test-set accuracy is computed over the instances linked to each identified weakness node.

TextDiff (Zhong et al., 2022).

TextDiff is an LLM-based method that automatically describes distributional differences between two text collections in natural language. We use it to generate a weakness profile by contrasting failed and successful cases (Figure 9). While not originally designed for weakness profiling, we adapt it by re-annotating development set instances with weakness labels: an LLM assigns each instance to one of the weakness capabilities identified in the weakness profile (Figure 10), yielding per-capability accuracy on the development set. We rank capabilities by ascending development-set accuracy to obtain the predicted weakness ordering, and evaluate each capability on its correspondingly labeled test instances.

QualEval (Murahari et al., 2024).

QualEval uses a two-stage LLM pipeline to derive a flat capability categorization from benchmark instances. In Stage 1, an LLM is prompted with a random sample of development-set instances to generate a predefined number of capability labels (Figure 7). We use the official implementation with its default hyperparameters. In Stage 2, an LLM scores the relevance of each capability to each instance (Figure 8), and a linear programming solver then assigns each instance to one or more of the discovered capabilities subject to coverage constraints. Weakness profiling selects capabilities with the lowest per-capability model accuracy on the development split as the predicted weaknesses. We rank capabilities by ascending development-set accuracy to obtain the predicted weakness ordering, and evaluate each capability’s test-set accuracy on its assigned instances. Because QualEval treats all discovered capabilities as potentially weak, its ranking spans all capabilities rather than a filtered subset.

SkillVerse (Tian et al., 2025).

SkillVerse is an unsupervised framework that organizes LLM behavior into a tree-structured dendrogram. Rather than operating on benchmark instances directly, it first collects model responses and invokes an LLM-as-judge to produce fine-grained critiques of each response on the development set (Figure 11). These critiques are parsed into atomic skill judgments (Figure 12), then embedded and hierarchically clustered into a dendrogram, where each node aggregates related behavioral observations at a chosen granularity. Model proficiency at each node is estimated from the proportion of favorable critiques among the associated responses. For weakness profiling, we identify nodes with below-threshold proficiency as weaknesses, using the default granularity and threshold from the official implementation. We use the proficiency scores to rank weaknesses and compute test-set accuracy on instances mapped to each weakness node via embedding similarity.

C.2 TIDE Implementation

C.2.1 Hyperparameter Settings

Unless stated otherwise, we use dmax=10d_{\max}\!=\!10, nmin=100n_{\min}\!=\!100, gmin=10−3g_{\min}\!=\!10^{-3}, C=10C\!=\!10, α=0.5\alpha\!=\!0.5, and β=1\beta\!=\!1, as in Section 4.4. Diagnostic extraction (Section 4.5) tests each node statistic against the corresponding root-level statistic using Clopper-Pearson exact binomial intervals at significance level αCI=0.05\alpha_{\mathrm{CI}}\!=\!0.05 with tolerance τ=0\tau\!=\!0. Concretely, in the single-model setting a node is declared weak when the upper confidence bound on s⁡(Bv)s(B_{v}) falls below s⁡(Broot)−τs(B_{\mathrm{root}})-\tau; in the multi-model setting a node is declared discriminative when the lower confidence bound on g⁡(Bv)g(B_{v}) exceeds g⁡(Broot)+τg(B_{\mathrm{root}})+\tau. The split-rule proposer (Figure 13) and the sample classifier (Figure 14) share the same backbone LLM, run at decoding temperature 00. Each split-rule-proposal call sees a batch of up to 1,0001{,}000 samples (a single LLM call per batch). Sample-to-group classification is parallelized across 150150 concurrent workers. Both stages cache outputs so that re-runs over the same node are inexpensive. Trees are constructed in breadth-first order, we verified separately that depth-first traversal yields the same tree and only affects compute scheduling. The main paper reports the α∈{0,1}\alpha\!\in\!\{0,1\} degeneracy ablation in Section 5.3.

Appendix D Experimental Analysis

D.1 Models and Datasets

We evaluate TIDE on four benchmarks chosen to span knowledge, reasoning, reading-comprehension, and social-bias regimes: MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), BBH (Suzgun et al., 2023), DROP (Dua et al., 2019), and BBQ (Parrish et al., 2022). For each benchmark we sample 3,0003{,}000 items and split them evenly into a development set and a held-out test set with a fixed random seed. All methods construct their trees or weakness profiles on the dev set only. Capability trees are reused across all evaluated models because the supervision signal is the multi-model behavior matrix, routing test items through the dev-time tree therefore reuses the same partition without re-induction. HLE-Verified is used only for the single-model qualitative analysis in Section D.2.

We evaluate five frontier model families: Grok 4.20, Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek-V3.2, GPT-5.4, and Qwen-Plus. All models are accessed through hosted APIs with default decoding settings. We record the exact model identifiers used in our release. The split-rule proposer and sample classifier inside TIDE use GPT-5.2 as the backbone unless otherwise stated, matching the baseline configuration described in Appendix C.1.

D.2 Additional Analysis

Single-Model Fine-Grained Capability Analysis.

Beyond the multi-model setting reported in the main paper, TIDE also provides a useful diagnostic lens for an individual model. Figures 5 visualize the per-leaf accuracy of Qwen3.6-Plus and Gemini-3.1-Pro on the TIDE tree induced over HLE-Verified. For both models, the weakest leaf falls substantially below the aggregate accuracy, and the spread across leaves is far wider than what the single scalar suggests, confirming that aggregate scores can mask large within-benchmark variation even for one model. The weak leaves correspond to coherent capability slices, such as references-heavy abstract physics and unit-conversion items for Qwen3.6-Plus, indicating that the induced partitions surface interpretable failure regions rather than statistical artifacts.

D.3 Case Studies

We include representative root-to-leaf paths that localize weaknesses invisible at the aggregate level. For a single-model setting, Table 4 lists the nodes of a representative TIDE tree, with each row reporting the node identifier, the natural-language description proposed by the split-rule proposer, and one example sample drawn from the node subset, while Table 5 reports the corresponding root-to-leaf paths and per-leaf accuracy. For a multi-model setting, Tables 6 and 7 report the analogous node-level descriptions and root-to-leaf paths, with the third column of Table 7 showing the per-leaf accuracy gap between two models. All four tables are placed at the end of the appendix because of their width, immediately after the prompt templates.

Appendix E Prompt Templates

For reproducibility, we list the full prompts used by every baseline as well as by TIDE. For each method we include every LLM stage of its pipeline, matching the procedure in Appendix C.1 and Appendix C.2, and report the prompts on a representative benchmark. Prompts on the other benchmarks differ only in the domain reference. EvalTree uses one capability-annotation prompt; QualEval uses Stage 1 capability discovery and Stage 2 relevance scoring; TextDiff uses weakness generation followed by instance annotation; SkillVerse uses Stage 1 critique generation and Stage 2 atomic judgment; TIDE uses splitting-rule discovery and sample assignment.
